summary.one_line: A 40-year-old, debt-free Manesar maker of geophone strings and seismic cables that is profitable but lumpy. Its revenue fell in FY26, cash flow halved and inventory is about one year of sales. The IPO funds mostly replacement machinery at a plant running far below capacity, and the company could have paid for that from its own cash before it spent it on buybacks and dividends.
bull_points: Debt-free: restated borrowings were nil at 31 March 2026 and 30 April 2026, apart from a token cash-credit balance (S3, S7).
Profit improved sharply over three years. PAT went from Rs 4.00 cr (FY24) to Rs 10.51 cr (FY25) to Rs 11.64 cr (FY26), and the PAT margin on operating revenue rose from 11.27% to 25.77% (S3).

A real, if small, niche with 40 years of history. It makes seismic sensors and cables in-house (extrusion, moulding, coil winding, magnetising, testing) under the 'HG' brand, which began as a collaboration with Geosource Inc., USA (S1, S5).
Diversified global customer base. In FY26, 84.22% of revenue came from exports to 47 countries, with the US (24.19%), Norway, Germany and Sweden the largest markets (S3).
bear_points: Revenue from operations fell about 8%, from Rs 49.08 cr in FY25 to Rs 45.16 cr in FY26. Operating cash flow fell 56% to Rs 6.14 cr while reported profit rose (S3, S15).
Inventory rose to Rs 45.33 cr at FY26 end, roughly equal to a full year's revenue, and the filing gives no operational reason for the build-up (S15).

Rs 19.36 cr of the identified proceeds goes to replacement machinery, a gold-plating line and building work. Yet utilisation in FY26 was only 13.63% for geophone strings and 24.32% for cables (units), and the company held about Rs 21.5 cr of cash and current investments at FY26 (S7, S13).
Concentrated revenue: the top customer was 21.79%, the top 5 were 60.21% and the top 10 were 72.58% of FY26 revenue, with no long-term contracts (S3).
No evident moat. India's largest seismic buyer, ONGC, ordered 24,000 SG-5 geophones from France's Sercel in October 2025 (S20).
watch_points: Final subscription mix at close on 3 November 2026. No category-wise figures were published as of the morning of day 1 (S19, S9).
Whether the inventory build converts to FY27 sales and cash. The April 2026 stub showed Rs 3.11 cr of revenue and Rs 3.28 cr of operating cash inflow (S3, S15).
Use of the unquantified 'unidentified acquisitions and general corporate purposes' bucket (S3, S16).
Customer concentration: sources disagree on how concentrated it is (top 10 at 72.58% versus 'about 90%'), so check the RHP (S3, S8).

reasoning: The new money does not fund growth the business visibly needs. Of the identified uses, Rs 15.05 cr is replacement machinery, Rs 1.05 cr a gold-plating line and Rs 3.26 cr building work. Management describes these as efficiency projects, not capacity additions, at a plant where most lines ran far below capacity in FY26 (S13, S17).

Capital allocation favours insiders over the IPO. The company spent Rs 13.04 cr on a buyback plus Rs 3.02 cr buyback tax in FY25 and paid Rs 7.68 cr of dividends in FY26, more than that year's Rs 6.14 cr operating cash flow. It still held about Rs 21.5 cr of cash and current investments, enough to cover nearly all of the Rs 19.36 cr of identified capex, yet it is raising public money and promoter-family members are selling Rs 6.65 cr through the OFS (S7, S1).

The growth story is not supported by the numbers. Revenue fell about 8% in FY26, operating cash flow fell 56%, and inventory rose 19% to Rs 45.33 cr (about one year of sales) with no stated reason. Profit growth that coincides with an inventory build and a sharp drop in material cost (Rs 14.95 cr to Rs 8.97 cr) needs explaining before it can be trusted (S3, S15).

No demonstrable moat. HGS is a small supplier in a market led by Sercel and Geospace. India's own ONGC sourced 24,000 geophones from Sercel in 2025, and the company makes no market-share or sole-supplier claim in any source we read (S20, S21, S22, S16).

The governance set-up is thin for a listed company. All three independent directors (aged 82 to 83) were appointed only in October 2025 ahead of the IPO, none has a formal education certificate on record, and the company cannot trace RoC allotment, balance-sheet and transfer records from 1986 onwards (S11, S12).

Concentrated and cyclical demand: the top 10 customers were 72.58% of FY26 revenue, there are no long-term contracts, and spending is tied to oil, gas and seabed survey budgets. One lost customer can swing a year (S3, S22).

subsections.title: What HGS makes and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: HGS (India) Limited was incorporated in February 1986 as 'Geosource India Limited', a technical and financial collaboration with Geosource Inc., USA, and was renamed in 1992 (S1, S24). It makes the sensing end of a seismic survey. Geophones are small coil-and-magnet sensors that convert ground vibration into an electrical signal. HGS wires them into geophone strings (harnesses), connects them through seismic cables and geophysical connectors, and also sells parts and accessories, all under the 'HG' brand (S1, S5). The same cables and connectors are also sold for resistivity meters and radar equipment (S18).

HGS supplies components and arrays, not complete recording systems. The products end up in oil and gas exploration, seabed geophysical surveys, mineral exploration, defence research, earthquake monitoring and vibration analysis (S1, S3). Sales are made against purchase orders that can be amended or cancelled, not under long-term contracts (S3, S17).

blocks.caption: FY 2025-26 revenue mix (restated, per RHP as summarised by S3 and S13)

blocks.text: The mix has shifted. Geophone strings rose from Rs 25.10 cr (51.15%) in FY25 to Rs 29.94 cr (66.29%) in FY26, while seismic cables fell from Rs 13.23 cr (26.95%) to Rs 9.21 cr (S13). The RHP attributes the FY26 revenue decline to lower sales of parts and accessories, seismic cables and connectors (S3). The balance row in the table is our arithmetic from the stated totals, not a disclosed figure.

One unexplained point: geophone-string revenue rose about 19% in FY26, but disclosed production of strings fell to 9,814 units (13.63% utilisation) from 27.07% utilisation in FY25 (S13). Shipments from earlier stock, a richer product mix or higher pricing could each explain this. The secondary sources do not say which.

HGS is mainly an exporter. Exports were Rs 38.04 cr, or 84.22% of FY26 revenue, up from 59.15% in FY25 (S3, S13). By country, the US was 24.19%, India 15.78%, Norway 13.58%, Germany 12.02% and Sweden 11.81% (S3). Overseas sales and service are supported by HGS Products B.V., a wholly owned Netherlands subsidiary set up in 2015 (S1, S3). An earlier disclosure cited 146 clients in 21 countries as of September 2025. The RHP-based summary refers to sales into about 47 countries by April 2026 (S4, S3).

Supply depends on imports. Imported material was 73.65% of FY26 raw-material purchases (Rs 12.32 cr of Rs 16.73 cr), up from 59.58% in FY24. The top 10 suppliers were 69.32% of purchases, and 99.04% in the April 2026 stub (S14). The main sources were India (26.35%), Belgium (25.72%, new in FY26), the Netherlands (19.60%) and the US (11.62%). Inputs are plastic granules, copper, brass, aluminium, steels and special conductors (S14). The company has no long-term supply agreements (S14).

Both ends of the business are exposed to currency moves. Revenue is mostly in foreign currency and inputs are mostly imported. Foreign-exchange fluctuation losses rose to Rs 1.06 cr in FY26 from Rs 0.37 cr in FY25 (S14). IPOWatch's summary of the RHP puts top-10 customer revenue at 'about 90%', which differs from the 72.58% in other summaries. We use 72.58% but flag the conflict (S8, S3).

All manufacturing is at one integrated plant in IMT Manesar, Haryana. The plant covers cable extrusion, injection moulding, precision assembly, coil winding, magnetising and test labs (S5, S1). It is a 100% Export Oriented Unit recognised by the Noida SEZ, holds ISO 9001:2015 (since 2005) and MSME ZED Gold (2024), and was recognised as a One Star Export House in 2010 (S1, S16). The company had 162 employees at 30 April 2026, and employee cost was Rs 15.24 cr in FY26, about a third of revenue (S3).

blocks.caption: Installed capacity and utilisation, certified by a chartered engineer on 15 Oct 2026 (S13, S17)

blocks.text: The plant is far larger than the business needs. Apart from parts and accessories, every line ran at a quarter of capacity or less in FY26, and connector and metre-cable capacity is barely used (S13). The RHP itself notes that installed capacity includes management assumptions and estimates (S17). This matters for the objects of the issue. The company is not short of capacity. Any case for the capex rests on efficiency and process control (S13).

One site, one product family, two-thirds of revenue: the single Manesar facility makes everything, and geophone strings are 66.29% of revenue. A disruption at the plant or a technology shift in how surveys are recorded would hit the whole company (S3).

HGS sells into the seismic data-acquisition equipment market. Demand there follows exploration budgets of oil and gas companies, offshore and seabed survey contractors, mining companies and research or defence agencies. Commercial research firms put the global geophone market at roughly US$2.5 billion in 2024, rising to about US$5 billion by 2034 (S23). These estimates vary widely between publishers and definitions, so treat them as directional only. None comes from the RHP, and the summaries we read did not reproduce the RHP's industry section.

The cyclicality is real and severe. Geospace Technologies, a listed US maker of geophones and seismic equipment, has repeatedly reported sharp drops in oil and gas segment revenue when exploration spending falls. It still made a net loss in fiscal 2024 on US$135.6 million of revenue, of which US$77.5 million came from oil and gas markets (S22). HGS's own history fits the pattern: revenue rose 38% in FY25, then fell 8% in FY26 (S3). Reviewers attribute the FY26 decline to cyclical, tender-driven ordering (S5, S6).

About 28% of FY26 revenue came from seabed geophysical survey and 20% from vibration monitoring, so HGS is not purely an oil and gas play (S3). Even so, oil and gas exploration is still about 28% of revenue and the biggest single swing factor.

Reviewers report that no listed Indian company does the same business, so there is no domestic listed comparable (S4). That does not mean there is no competition. The global market is led by Sercel (part of France's Viridien group), which calls itself 'the leading designer and manufacturer of precision sensors' and sells the SG-5, SG-10 Neo and JF-30DX geophone ranges (S21). Geospace Technologies in the US is the other large established maker (S22). The RHP itself cites competition from 'Indian and multinational seismic-equipment suppliers' without naming them (S16).

In October 2025, India's biggest seismic buyer, ONGC, ordered three Sercel 528 recording systems with 24,000 channels and 24,000 SG-5 geophones for its 2026 season (S20). This fits HGS's own revenue mix, where India is only 15.78% of sales (S3). HGS seems to win business mainly as a component and harness supplier to overseas survey and equipment firms, not as the default domestic supplier.

blocks.text: We found no evidence of a durable moat. None of the sources we read reports a market-share claim, a sole-supplier or import-substitution position, a patent portfolio or a regulatory licence that keeps rivals out (S16, S8). The stated strengths are a wide product range, about 40 years of experience, long customer relationships and established vendors (S8). Most prospectuses list similar strengths.

items: What is real: four decades of continuous manufacturing, in-house extrusion, moulding and magnetising, ISO 9001 since 2005, and repeat export customers in demanding markets such as Norway, Germany and the US (S16, S3).
What is not a moat: EOU status, ZED Gold and an SME award are certifications that peers can obtain too (S16).
Counter-evidence: high customer concentration with no long-term contracts, and the domestic flagship buyer sourcing from Sercel, point to a price-taking component supplier (S3, S20).

blocks.text: Verdict on moat: none demonstrated. HGS appears to be a competent niche contract manufacturer whose relationships carry some switching cost. It does not appear to have pricing power or a protected market position.

blocks.caption: Restated consolidated financials, Rs crore (S3, S1, S2)

blocks.text: The headline trend is positive: PAT nearly tripled from FY24 to FY26 and margins widened every year (S3). But FY26 revenue fell while profit rose. Two drivers stand out. Cost of materials consumed fell from Rs 14.95 cr to Rs 8.97 cr, which is far more than the 8% revenue drop (S3). And other income was a large share of profit: total income minus operating revenue was about Rs 3.75 cr in FY26 and Rs 4.37 cr in FY25 (our arithmetic from S15 and S3), against FY26 profit before tax of Rs 15.42 cr (S7).

Chanakya Nipothi's review makes the same point: higher profit on lower income 'warrants examination of other income and recurring earnings' (S6). Some sources compute margins on total income (FY26 PAT margin 23.79%, not 25.77%) (S5). We use revenue from operations as the denominator, consistent with the RHP KPIs (S3).

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash-flow items, Rs crore (S7, S15, S3, S1)

blocks.text: The balance sheet has no debt, but the working capital is heavy. Inventory of Rs 45.33 cr at FY26 was roughly equal to that year's Rs 45.16 cr of revenue, and it absorbed Rs 7.37 cr of cash in FY26 after releasing Rs 4.42 cr in FY25 (S15). Per the analysis we read, 'the financial statements do not disclose the operational reason for the increase' (S15). Receivables are small (Rs 3.85 cr), so the cash problem is stock, not customers paying late (S7).

Operating cash flow fell 56% to Rs 6.14 cr while PAT rose to Rs 11.64 cr. Over FY26, cash conversion was only about half of reported profit (S15). The April 2026 stub was better, with an operating inflow of Rs 3.28 cr helped by a Rs 2.10 cr fall in receivables (S15). One month is too short to call this a reversal.

Two definitions of equity are in use. The KPI 'net worth' (Rs 89.27 cr FY26) is lower than share capital plus reserves (Rs 99.19 cr). The summaries do not reconcile the gap, and reserves alone (Rs 90.66 cr) exceed the KPI figure (S7, S1). Investors should read the RHP's definition before relying on either figure.

subsections.title: Capital allocation and quality of earnings

blocks.text: Before this IPO, HGS returned a lot of cash to existing shareholders. FY25 saw a buyback of Rs 13.04 cr plus Rs 3.02 cr buyback tax and Rs 4.27 cr of dividends. FY26 saw Rs 7.68 cr of dividends, about 66% of PAT and Rs 1.54 cr more than operating cash flow (S7). Share capital fell from Rs 9.48 cr to Rs 7.11 cr in FY25 and then rose to Rs 8.53 cr in FY26 (S7). The buyback explains why net worth dipped in FY25 despite Rs 10.51 cr of profit. The share-capital increase in FY26 is not explained in the sources we read.

items: The FY25 buyback and FY24 to FY26 dividends total about Rs 31 cr of cash paid out (our sum of S7 figures). That is more than the Rs 19.36 cr of identified capex the IPO is now funding (S13).
Cash plus current investments of about Rs 21.5 cr at FY26 (S7) could have covered most of the stated projects without new equity.
Margins rose as material cost fell and inventory built up, a pattern that needs the RHP notes to rule out timing effects (S3, S15).

blocks.text: The numbers do not support the growth story yet. FY26 shows falling revenue, halved operating cash flow, a year's worth of inventory and payouts larger than cash generation. That is not a business that needs public equity to grow. It is one whose owners have taken cash out and are now asking the public to fund maintenance capex.

blocks.caption: Offer structure at the upper band of Rs 120 (S1, S5, S3)

blocks.text: This is a book-built NSE SME issue with a price band of Rs 114 to 120 and face value Rs 10. Bidding runs from 30 October to 3 November 2026, with tentative allotment on 4 November and listing on 6 November (S1, S5). The minimum individual bid is 2 lots of 1,200 shares (2,400 shares, Rs 2.88 lakh at the upper band). Small HNIs bid 3 to 6 lots, and big HNIs start at 7 lots (S1, S2). The net offer is split QIB up to 50%, retail at least 35% and NII at least 15% (S1). Hem Securities is the book-running lead manager and KFin Technologies the registrar (S1).
Shares outstanding rise from 85,32,713 to 1,08,58,713 (S1). Of the total issue, about 19% is OFS, and all of that money goes to the sellers, not the company (S1).

Sources differ on the price band: the RHP-based analysis says the RHP itself leaves the band blank (S16), and aggregators report Rs 114 to 120 (S1, S2, S18). Several aggregators label the fresh issue differently (Rs 26.17 cr excluding the market-maker portion versus Rs 27.91 cr including it) (S2, S5). The share counts above reconcile.

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds per RHP-based sources, Rs crore (S3, S13, S1)
rows: Replacement of plant and machinery, Manesar
Unidentified acquisitions and general corporate purposes

blocks.text: The replacement machinery list covers multi-spindle winding machines, an automatic lathe, laser marking, an extrusion line, a buncher, moulding machines, soldering stations, QC gauges, magnetisers, ovens and microscopes (S13). Gold plating is currently done by outside labs, and the Rs 1.05 cr line is intended to give better control over quality and cost (S13). The building work is meant to bring departments together and cut material movement (S13). Management frames all of this as replacement and efficiency, not as an addition to installed capacity (S13). The cost estimates are internal and have not been appraised by a bank or financial institution (S3).

By our arithmetic, the gross fresh issue of Rs 27.91 cr minus the Rs 19.36 cr identified leaves roughly Rs 8.5 cr. That residual covers issue expenses plus the unidentified acquisitions and general corporate purposes bucket. The secondary sources do not give the split (S5, S13).

Sources disagree on two details. IPOWatch lists Rs 18.50 cr for machinery and Rs 4.73 cr for building work, which is probably DRHP-stage data (S4). Sources also disagree on whether the building work is on the second or third floor (S13, S1). We use the RHP-based figures (S3, S13). Note also that money set aside for 'unidentified acquisitions' gives management discretion without disclosure.

subsections.title: Offer for sale and who is selling

blocks.text: About 84% of the OFS shares are sold by members of the founding Singh family and promoter group. Pawan Singh and Anjali Singh, the two largest sellers, are also shareholders of the corporate promoter Sowar (S1, S10). This is a modest stake sale, but it adds to the FY25 buyback and the dividends already paid. The family is taking cash out at the same time as new capital comes in.

The four named promoters are Anil Dass, Shashi Singh, Cecilia Margareta Singh Ramel and Sowar Private Limited. Together they hold 57,62,032 shares (67.53%) before the offer and about 53.06% after it (S10, S3). Including the wider promoter group, the pre-issue holding is 87.30% (S1). Sowar alone holds 47.82% before and 37.58% after the offer (S3). Sowar was incorporated in 1980 and lists medical-equipment trading and servicing plus oil, gas and mineral exploration consultancy as its business (S10).

Control is spread across a family group. Cecilia Ramel inherited her HGS shares, and her largest stake in Sowar (37.78%), when the original promoter, the late Major Brijendra Singh, her husband, died on 30 September 2025 (S10). Shashi Singh, his brother, holds 23.50% of Sowar and is its managing director. Anil Dass holds 17.49% (S10). The sources disclose no shareholder agreement or voting arrangement between the families (S10).

blocks.caption: Post-issue lock-in (S3)
rows: 23,46,000 Sowar shares (21.60% of post-offer capital), minimum promoter contribution

blocks.text: Anil Dass has been on the board since incorporation and is Managing Director. Dhiraj Kumar Vashista is a whole-time director (since April 2024) and also CFO, and Samir Gugnani has been a whole-time director since 2011. Malti Sen chairs the board as a non-executive director, and Shashi Singh is also a non-executive director (S11). Anil Dass also sits on the boards of Sowar, SGSIL Geophysical Services Pvt Ltd and HGS (India) Sales and Services Pvt Ltd, so the group has common directorships across several entities (S26). Management has run the company for decades, which counts in its favour. The sources do not describe any separate ventures with a public track record.

All three independent directors (Ravi Indra Singh Verdi, Dileep Rao and Ravinder Singh Sodhi, aged 82 to 83) were appointed on 29 October 2025, five months before the DRHP was filed. Two are retired Army officers and one is retired from ITC. None holds shares, and none has a formal education certificate available (S11). The audit committee was formed only on 12 February 2026 (S11). The board is legally compliant, but it was assembled for the listing and is unlikely to act as a strong check on the founding families.

Compliance history: HGS cannot trace allotment returns for 13 allotments (1986 to 1997), balance-sheet filings for FY1987 to FY1998, annual returns for FY1987 to FY2002, auditor-appointment forms for FY1987 to FY2013, and several share transfer and transmission records. A practising company secretary's search in March 2026 did not find them. The company believes the forms were filed on time but discloses no remediation, and it does not quantify any penalty exposure (S12).

items: Loan to the promoter: HGS lent Rs 9.50 cr to Sowar in FY24. It was repaid as Rs 1.50 cr in FY24 and Rs 8.00 cr in FY25, with Rs 13.42 lakh of interest received in FY25 (S3).
Consultancy and management fees paid to Sowar: Rs 9.75 lakh in FY26 (S3).
MD remuneration: Anil Dass received Rs 1.16 cr in FY26, plus Rs 15.89 lakh of accrued commission (S3).
Independent directors' sitting fees totalled Rs 1.90 lakh in FY26, and the Netherlands subsidiary paid no director remuneration (S11).

blocks.text: The ongoing related-party flows are small and look routine. The one item that matters is the Rs 9.50 cr loan to Sowar, the promoter holding company, in FY24, which was more than double that year's PAT of Rs 4.00 cr (S3). It was repaid with interest, but it shows that company cash has been used for promoter-entity needs. Investors should expect the post-listing audit committee to stop this. The sources we read do not mention any promoter-linked supplier or customer.

Litigation is minor. The company uses a materiality threshold of Rs 11.64 lakh (S27). It faces a Rs 15.28 lakh civil appeal by Remya Fashions, a former employee's reinstatement claim, and five tax matters totalling Rs 6.04 lakh. Promoters and directors face six direct-tax claims of Rs 13.09 lakh, and Sowar is the plaintiff in a Rs 25.18 lakh civil suit against DHBVN (S3). None of these is material to a business with about Rs 99 cr of equity (S7).

items: Customer concentration with no contracts: the top customer was 21.79% and the top 10 were 72.58% of FY26 revenue. Orders can be amended or cancelled, and the top-10 share jumped from 56.24% a year earlier (S3, S13).

Product and end-market concentration: geophone strings were 66.29% of revenue, and demand depends on exploration and survey budgets that have historically fallen 24% to 64% in down-years for peers (S3, S22).
Inventory and cash conversion: Rs 45.33 cr of inventory (about one year of sales) with no stated reason. If it is slow-moving, the high FY26 margins could reverse through write-downs (S15).
Import and currency exposure: 73.65% of purchases are imported, the top 10 suppliers account for 69.32%, and FX losses were Rs 1.06 cr in FY26 (S14).
Geopolitical and trade exposure: the US was 24.19% of revenue, and the company discloses exposure to conflict-related disruption, though none had been material as of the RHP date (S3).

blocks.text: The concentration risks stack on each other. In practice one site, one product family, a handful of customers and a cyclical end market make up most of the business. A single lost account in a weak exploration year could cut revenue by a fifth (S3).

items: Execution and value of capex: Rs 19.36 cr goes to replacement and efficiency projects, not new capacity, at a plant with low utilisation. The return on this spend is not quantified, and the estimates have not been appraised (S13, S3).
Unquantified 'unidentified acquisitions and GCP' bucket: this gives management discretion over part of the proceeds with no disclosed target (S3, S6).

Governance depth: the independent directors were all appointed in October 2025, statutory records since 1986 are missing, and there is history of a large loan to the promoter holding company (S11, S12, S3).

SME liquidity: trading is in 1,200-share lots with a single market maker, and about 21.6% of post-issue capital is locked for 3 years. Other pre-issue promoter shares are locked for only 1 to 2 years and non-promoter pre-issue shares for 1 year, so supply could rise after those dates (S5, S3).

blocks.text: We leave out the generic RHP boilerplate risks (economic slowdown, changes in tax law, pandemic and similar). The risks above are the ones specific enough to change a decision on this issue.

We found no explicit forward guidance from management: no revenue or margin target, no order-book disclosure and no investor call or interview. The RHP-based analysis we read states this directly (S3, S17). Management's stated plans are the projects funded by the issue (S16).

items: Replace and modernise machinery at Manesar over FY27 to FY28 to improve efficiency (S13).
Bring gold plating and thickness verification in-house, both outsourced today, for quality and cost control (S13).
Develop the additional floor at Manesar to bring departments together and add an assembly line (S13).
Raise production volumes to absorb fixed costs, and manage supply-chain cost through inventory levels and economic order quantities (S13).
Possibly pursue unidentified acquisitions (S16).

blocks.text: Without an order book or guidance, the only forward data point is the April 2026 stub: Rs 3.11 cr of revenue and Rs 1.11 cr of PAT in one month. That is too short a period for a seasonal, order-driven business to show a trend (S3).

The plans support modest margin improvement at best. Nothing disclosed points to a step-change in revenue. The installed base can already produce far more than it sells, so growth depends on winning orders, not on capex (S13). FY27 will mainly show whether the FY26 inventory build turns into revenue.

Seabed survey and vibration-monitoring demand gives some diversification away from oil and gas (S3). However, India's flagship exploration buyer chose a foreign supplier for its 2026 season (S20), so there is no evidence of a domestic tailwind specific to HGS.

Reviewers' optimism ('May Apply', 'Selective Apply') rests on profit growth and a low price. We exclude price by design, and neither review identifies a concrete growth driver beyond the capex (S8, S6).

This report was written on the opening day. As of our check, the main trackers had not published any category-wise subscription data. Chittorgarh stated that subscription information was 'not available at this time', and IPO Ji showed data pending (S19, S9). No QIB, NII or retail figures exist yet, and nothing should be inferred about demand.

Anchor bidding was scheduled for 29 October 2026 (S18). IPO Ji lists an anchor reservation of 8,13,600 shares (S9), and the RHP-based summary describes the anchor portion as 60% of the QIB category, with one-third reserved for domestic mutual funds (S16). We found no announcement of anchor investor names, the amount raised or the lock-in end dates. The trackers still showed these as blank (S4).
Grey market premium (unofficial, unregulated): reported at Rs 0 (0%) as of 27 to 30 October 2026 (S5, S2). This is not an investment signal and played no part in our verdict.

method: Researched on 30 October 2026, the opening day of the issue. MATERIAL GAP: we could not read the primary offer documents directly. The company-hosted RHP dated 26 October 2026 (S25) returned a bot-verification page, and the NSE Emerge-hosted DRHP (S24) timed out twice. Both were confirmed to exist through search results. All RHP content in this report therefore comes from secondary sources that summarise the RHP: mainly Multibagg AI's series of RHP-based articles (S3, S7, S10 to S17), checked against aggregator pages (Chittorgarh S1, InvestorGain S2, IPO Watch S4, Pocketly S5, IPO Ji S9) and an independent review (Chanakya Nipothi S6). Headline financials (total income, EBITDA, PAT, net worth, total assets) match across at least four independent pages. Where sources conflicted, we chose and flagged as follows: top-10 customer share (72.58% versus 'about 90%'), the objects amounts (RHP-stage Rs 15.05/1.05/3.26 cr versus Rs 18.50/4.73 cr in IPO Watch, probably DRHP-stage), the building floor (second versus third), promoter holding (67.53% for the named promoters versus 87.30% including the promoter group), and the KPI 'net worth' versus shareholders' funds. One source table misaligned utilisation years, and we used the version consistent with disclosed production units (9,814 strings, or 13.63% in FY26). Industry sizing comes from commercial research summaries seen in search results (S23) and is low-reliability. The competitor context comes from Sercel/Viridien primary pages (S20, S21) and a Geospace earnings summary (S22). Some sources (S22, S23, S26, S27) were seen only in search results, not opened. Dates on secondary pages are our access date where no publication date was shown. Margins are computed on revenue from operations. Figures marked 'our arithmetic' are derived, not disclosed. As required, valuation (P/E, P/B, market-cap multiples, peer multiples) is deliberately excluded. No subscription, anchor allocation or credible GMP data beyond a reported Rs 0 existed at the time of writing.
